evidence.quote: they knew how to weave stuffs of the most beautiful colors and elaborate patterns, the clothes manufactured from which should have the wonderful property of remaining invisible to everyone who was unfit for the office he held, or who was extraordinarily simple in character
evidence.paraphrase: The weavers claim their cloth has a special property: it is invisible to anyone unfit for office or foolish.

evidence.quote: "What can be the meaning of this?" thought the old man, opening his eyes very wide. "I cannot discover the least bit of thread on the looms."
evidence.paraphrase: The old minister is astonished that he can see nothing on the looms.

evidence.quote: "Is it possible that I am a simpleton? I have never thought so myself; and no one must know it now if I am so."
evidence.paraphrase: The minister worries that his inability to see the cloth means he is a simpleton, and resolves to hide it.

evidence.quote: "How is this?" said the Emperor to himself. "I can see nothing! This is indeed a terrible affair! Am I a simpleton, or am I unfit to be an Emperor?"
evidence.paraphrase: The Emperor is alarmed that he cannot see the cloth and fears it means he is unfit.

evidence.quote: and at the same time they pointed to the empty frames; for they imagined that everyone else could see this exquisite piece of workmanship.
evidence.paraphrase: The narration reveals to the reader that the frames are empty, contrasting with the characters' praise.

evidence.quote: "But the Emperor has nothing at all on!" said a little child.
evidence.paraphrase: A child openly states the truth that the Emperor is wearing nothing.

evidence.quote: "But he has nothing at all on!" at last cried out all the people. The Emperor was vexed, for he knew that the people were right; but he thought the procession must go on now!
evidence.paraphrase: The whole crowd acknowledges the truth aloud, and the Emperor privately admits the people are right.
